name: Promiseline — the AI expeditor for hardware teams without an ERP
one_liner: For the mechanical/ops lead at a 20-150 person hardware startup (robotics, space, defense, devices) buying custom machined and fabricated parts from 10-40 independent shops, Promiseline forwards-and-chases: you BCC your POs to it, and an agent emails each shop on a cadence, reads the replies, maintains a confidence-scored promise date per line, and tells you which build or test milestone is now at risk — with no ERP, no supplier portal and no supplier login.
problem: Hardware teams below the ERP line run their outside-parts supply chain on a Google Sheet, Gmail and memory. A 20-150 person robotics/space/defense company typically has dozens to low hundreds of open PO lines across 10-40 shops (machining, sheet metal, anodize, plating, PCBA, castings). Every line has a promised date that the shop gave verbally or in a quote PDF, and that date is quietly wrong a meaningful share of the time: industry sources put US metal-fabricator average on-time delivery around 84% (FMA, cited 2026), and a manufacturing analysis of aerospace/drone parts claims ~40% of orders arrive late or with quality issues. Forum evidence from r/hwstartups and r/Machinists shows the same story in the first person: prototype buyers waiting months past a quoted date with no updates, teams losing track of part revisions and POs across separate spreadsheets, and weeks of manual supplier chasing. Today the fix is a human: a procurement/logistics coordinator ($62-72k posted at hardware startup Last Lock), a manufacturing expeditor ($44-55k), or an offshore procurement VA ($520-1,600/month) whose whole job is sending "any update on PO 1047?" emails and retyping replies into a sheet. That fails because the chasing is bursty and low-status, so it gets dropped the week before a build; because a shop saying "still on track" is not evidence; and because nobody links the slipping line back to the integration build or customer demo it blocks until the parts don't show up.
target_customer: Buyer: the VP Hardware / Director of Manufacturing / first Supply Chain hire at a 20-150 person venture-backed hardware company (robotics, space, defense, medical devices, industrial equipment) in the US. They own the build schedule and the vendor budget. They have no ERP, or an ERP they don't trust for outside processing; they have Gmail/Outlook, a parts sheet, and maybe Duro or Onshape. Secondary buyer: the contract-manufacturing ops lead at a 10-50 person CM who resells machining.
why_now: Three things changed. (1) The follow-up itself is now automatable: long-context models reliably parse a shop's one-line email reply ("pushed to the 19th, material came in short") into a structured date change with a reason, which is exactly the "$15-an-Hour Expert" pattern YC is asking for — AI doing the specialist coordination work an expeditor used to do (https://www.ycombinator.com/rfs#the-15-an-hour-expert). (2) The buyer population exploded: YC's own Fall 2026 batch includes twentyfour26 building autonomous CNC for "robotics, space, defense" prototype teams (https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Whg-twentyfour26-building-fully-autonomous-factories-in-america), and a16z's American Dynamism theses ("renaissance of the American factory", "building the AI-native industrial base", https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-2/) describe hundreds of newly funded hardware companies that all buy custom parts and none of which have a procurement department. (3) The incumbent layer just priced itself out of them: SourceDay starts around $30k/year per G2 and needs supplier portal adoption; Didero raised $30M Series A and positions at mid-market/enterprise; Leverage AI targets mid-market ERP users (SAP, NetSuite, Epicor, Infor). The sub-200-person, no-ERP buyer is explicitly not their customer.
comparables: SourceDay (sourceday.com) — PO collaboration and "Open Order Chaser"; G2 lists entry pricing around $30k/year and reviewers complain suppliers don't log into the portal, leaving buyers emailing anyway. Gap: price and portal dependence rule out small teams. Didero (didero.ai) — AI procurement agents for supplier comms and ERP updates; ~$37M raised ($7M seed + $30M Series A co-led by Chemistry and Headline), explicitly 100+ mid-market/enterprise deployments, sits on top of an ERP. Gap: assumes an ERP and an enterprise sales cycle. Leverage AI (tryleverage.ai) — email-based supplier follow-up with no portal/EDI, which is the closest mechanic to Promiseline, but positioned at mid-market manufacturers/distributors on SAP, NetSuite, Dynamics, Epicor, Infor, quote-only pricing. Gap: no self-serve, no no-ERP path, no link to a build schedule. Akisto (akisto.ai) — SF, founded 2026, AI supplier coordinator chasing open POs; site still says "Coming Soon" with a reported pilot on 2,000+ POs. This is the sharpest direct threat and should be watched closely; it reads as pre-launch and ERP/spreadsheet-import oriented rather than build-milestone oriented. Cofactr (cofactr.com) — strong for electronic components, adjusts lead times from supplier shipping history, but centred on distributor parts, not custom machining jobs with quote revisions and inspection steps. Xometry / Fictiv — give excellent tracking only for work ordered through their own networks, not for the buyer's own shops. HappyRobot — voice/email ops agent for manufacturers/suppliers, reportedly $150M Series C Aug 2026 at $1.2B, enterprise custom pricing. Kaizen Labs (kaizenlabs.co.in) — narrow PO email follow-up, pilot-priced, US presence unverified. The uncovered gap is consistent across all of them: the buyer with no ERP, under 200 people, who needs the answer expressed as "which build slips", sold self-serve for hundreds not tens of thousands.
market_note: Estimate, stated as such. There are plausibly several thousand US venture-backed hardware companies in the 20-150 person band plus tens of thousands of small CMs and equipment makers; if 3,000 are addressable in year 1-3 and 8% buy at $600/month, that is ~$17M ARR — a real but not enormous SMB wedge, which is why the expansion path matters (upward into the same company's first ERP years, sideways into incoming inspection and supplier scorecards). Willingness to pay is anchored on confirmed labour prices, not guesses: procurement VAs at $520-1,600/month (VAmasters, Wing at $999 part-time / $1,599 full-time), outsourced procurement at $8-25 per PO or $1,200-8,000/month, in-house coordinators at $62-72k. $400-900/month for software that removes the chasing is comfortably below the cheapest human. Note the counter-evidence: no source found shows a sub-200-person hardware team already paying for software for this specific job, so willingness to pay is inferred from labour substitution and must be tested with paid pilots.
risks: 1) Akisto and Leverage AI are already in this mechanic; if either drops a self-serve, no-ERP tier at $300-600/month the wedge narrows fast — speed and the build-milestone framing are the only defence. 2) The buyer may be too small and too few: a 40-person robotics company with 60 open lines may genuinely tolerate a sheet plus a $70k coordinator, and churn when they hire that person or install an ERP. 3) Supplier email replies are the data source; shops that answer by phone, or answer "on track" reflexively, produce a dashboard that is confidently wrong — the product has to score confidence honestly (last-contact age, specificity of the reply, that shop's historical slip) rather than show green.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) That the mechanical/ops lead will hand their supplier inbox to an agent that emails their shops under their domain — relationship risk is the biggest adoption blocker, more than price; mitigate with draft-and-approve mode for the first weeks. 2) That shops reply to automated chase emails at a usable rate (needs >50% reply within 3 days to beat a human); unverified. 3) That buyers pay $400-900/month for software when the alternative is a $520/month VA who also does other work — no source found shows a sub-200-person team paying for this category today.
first_customers: Named, findable this week: (a) YC Fall 2026 / Summer 2026 hardware companies — twentyfour26's own customers are literally "hardware companies in and around the Bay Area"; scrape the YC directory for Industrials/Robotics/Space and email the ops or founding-hardware person. (b) Companies currently hiring the role the product replaces — Last Lock (Procurement & Logistics Coordinator, $62-72k), Mach Industries (Procurement Specialist, $25-39/hr), Salient Motion (Buyer), Valar Atomics (Sr Buyer, expediting long-lead equipment), The Nuclear Company (Project Procurement Manager): a live job post is the strongest buying signal available and these are public. (c) r/hwstartups and the Hardware Startups / Hardware Massive Slack communities, where the "chasing shops" complaints are already posted. (d) Hardware-focused funds' portfolio pages (Eclipse, Lux, Root, Khosla hardware cos) for warm intros.
validation_test: This week, run a concierge expeditor on one real company. Offer three hardware startups found via the job posts above: "give me your open-PO sheet and a forwarding alias; for two weeks I will chase every shop and send you a Monday risk list naming which build each late line blocks. $250 for the pilot." Pass signal: at least 2 of 3 pay the $250 (not just say yes), supplier reply rate to the chase emails exceeds 50% within three days, and at least one date change is surfaced that the buyer did not already know about. Fail signal: they'll take it free but won't pay, or the shops ignore the emails, or every reply is "on track" with no new information. Running it by hand also produces the email templates and the slip taxonomy the agent will need.
build_plan: Narrowest sellable v1, 2-4 weeks of evenings for a TS/agent builder: (1) A forwarding inbox (po@customer.promiseline.com) plus a one-screen paste/CSV import for open PO lines: part number, rev, qty, shop, PO date, promised date, the build it feeds. (2) A scheduled agent (cron + model API) that drafts a short, human-sounding chase email per line on a cadence keyed to days-to-promise, sends from the buyer's own domain via Gmail/Outlook OAuth, and starts in draft-and-approve mode. (3) A reply parser that turns the shop's free-text answer into {new_date, reason, confidence, evidence_quote} and writes it to the line, keeping the original promise so slip history accumulates per shop. (4) The Monday Risk List: one email and one web page ranking lines by "days of build slip caused", with a confidence badge driven by reply age, reply specificity and that shop's historical slip. (5) Billing at $499/month for up to 150 open lines. CUT for v1: ERP and PLM integrations, any supplier login, voice calls, quoting, RFQ distribution, quote comparison, inspection/FAI, mobile app, multi-user permissions, and any attempt to predict dates with ML — the confidence score is explainable rules only.
launch_post:
Your machine shop said "on track." It wasn't.

Promiseline BCCs your POs, emails every shop on a cadence, reads the replies, and every Monday tells you one thing: which build slips, and because of which part.

No ERP. No supplier portal. No login for your shops.
reasoning:
This beat the others on the one thing that matters: a named buyer whose workaround has a published price. Every rival candidate either had no budget holder (npm cooldown tooling — the people in pain are developers, the budget sits with an AppSec team already being sold StepSecurity and Socket, and it is close to past ideas Strangers/SkillProof), was already well served (quoting — Forgepoint raised $9.8M in Oct 2026 for exactly the shop-side RFQ desk, and Paperless Parts owns the category), or was a signal restated as an idea (AI for City Hall, data-center supply chain).

It is not a repeat. The library's closest neighbours are Outbound (buyer at a 10-80 person machine shop managing outgoing vendor POs for heat-treat/plating, with spec flow-down as the core workflow) and HoldLine (an AI phone caller for B2B back offices). Promiseline sits on the other side of the table — the hardware company buying from shops, not the shop buying from processors — and its core artefact is a build-milestone risk list driven by email reply parsing, not a compliant vendor PO and not a phone call. Different buyer, different workflow, different wedge.

Fit with this builder is unusually good: it is an agent orchestration problem (scheduled chase, reply parse, state machine per PO line) in TypeScript with model APIs and no heavy infrastructure, which is exactly the UiPath-Maestro-shaped work they already do, and the first version is an inbox plus a cron plus one screen.

The honest discount: Akisto is doing something very close and may be ahead, and the willingness-to-pay for software — as opposed to for the VA this replaces — is inferred, not observed. That is why this is 7.8 and not 8.5, and why the validation test is a paid concierge pilot rather than a build.

candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Promiseline — AI expeditor for no-ERP hardware teams, output framed as "which build slips". PICK. Only candidate with a named buyer, a published workaround price, and a gap the incumbents state in their own positioning.
2. Cooldown proxy / dependency quarantine-as-a-service for 5-50 dev teams (from the Cable/Scott Wu bookmark). Finalist, lost. Screening + deep call found StepSecurity ($16/contributing dev/mo with cooldowns in Secure Registry), Socket ($25-50/user/mo), Endor, JFrog Curation already selling this exact control; also too close to past ideas Strangers and SkillProof.
3. Shop-side AI quoting desk — RFQ email to draft quote for sub-50-person job shops (from twentyfour26). Finalist, lost. Forgepoint raised $9.8M seed Oct 2026 from Primary and a16z speedrun for precisely this ("Frank", the AI inside sales rep), on top of Paperless Parts. Gap closed by a funded player at the same buyer.
4. Buyer-side quote normaliser — five shop PDFs into one comparison table for hardware buyers. Dropped at screen. MESH Works, Bourne and RFQmatch already claim it, and it is a once-per-project event rather than a weekly recurring pain, so no retention.
5. Long-lead equipment expediting for data-center developers (YC "Data Center Supply Chain" signal). Dropped at screen. Pain and budget are real (transformers 100-150+ weeks, switchgear 52-104 weeks) but the buyer is an EPC with a 9-18 month procurement cycle and incumbent project-controls software — far too long a first sale for an evenings-and-weekends start. Same mechanic as Promiseline, worse entry point; keep as the expansion market.
6. AS9102 / FAI ballooning for small shops. Dropped at screen. Real measured pain (2-5 hours per drawing) but InspectionXpert, High QA, Net-Inspect and Ideagen all own it and customers often mandate a specific tool.
7. Customer-facing job-status portal sold to small CNC shops ("stop the where's-my-part calls"). Dropped at screen. Research found only vendor marketing for the pain, no owner willingness-to-pay evidence, and JobBOSS already bundles a portal; it is the mirror image of Promiseline with a poorer buyer.
8. Outbound deliverability guardrail for AI SDR agents — pause the agent before the domain burns (from the Explee bookmark). Dropped at screen. Google Postmaster is free, GlockApps/Warmy/InboxAlly crowd the monitoring layer, and the buyer is a founder who just bought the cheap outbound tool.
9. MFD/RIA back-office agent for Indian mutual-fund distributors (from the sipsea bookmark + a16z "Wealth management for all"). Dropped at screen. Dense incumbent field (Wealth Elite, Investwell, NJ, Prudent), commission-sharing distribution model, and far from this builder's market access.
10. "Cognitive surrender" audit trail — proof-of-review logging for AI-generated work (from the Osmani bookmark). Dropped at screen. Latent pain, no budget holder, no recurring event; a compliance product looking for a regulation that does not exist yet.

PROJECT
(the project scout did not finish)
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3/3): summarised Explee (outbound agent, $30 credits, ~$0.04/email, self-reported 76k leads), twentyfour26 (YC Fall 2026, STEP-file-in autonomous CNC for robotics/space/defense prototype buyers, ~48h turnaround, reported $500k note) and the Jack Cable security guide (7-day minimum package age, pin + lockfile, Oct 29 malicious Cursor/Claude Code extension). Also resolved the Addy Osmani article (cognitive offloading → deferral → surrender). These produced candidates 1-3, 8 and 10; twentyfour26 is what pointed at the buyer side of custom-parts sourcing rather than the shop side.

Screening pot (6/6): npm cooldown vendors; machine-shop quoting software and benchmarks; AI-permit/city-hall; AI RFQ startups (this surfaced Forgepoint's $9.8M seed and killed candidate 3); AI-slop/outbound fatigue; Indian MFD software. Net effect: three candidates died at screen and the shop side of manufacturing was eliminated, pushing the search to the buyer side.

Deep-research pot (12/12): buyer-side sourcing tools (Xometry/Fictiv/Protolabs only track their own network); Forgepoint detail; data-center long-lead expediting and who owns it; third-party expediting firms and expeditor salaries; hardware-startup procurement stack (Cofactr, Duro); AI supplier-follow-up agents (HappyRobot, Kaizen Labs); FAI/AS9102; shop-side status portals; OTD benchmarks (FMA 84% average for fabricators, top quartile >90%); supplier slippage and hardware-startup expeditor job posts (Last Lock $62-72k, Integrated Magnetics $44-55k); promise-date confidence scoring; customer status-inquiry load. This is where the idea moved from "quoting" to "promise dates" and from "generic expeditor" to "no-ERP hardware buyer".

Sharpening pot (5/5): SourceDay pricing/complaints + the Morsa competitor list (SourceDay, Leverage, Didero, Coupa, SAP Business Network); Didero and Leverage positioning and funding; hwstartups/Machinists forum evidence on late parts and chasing; Akisto and no-ERP forward-email workflows; Leverage AI's no-portal/no-EDI mechanic and target size. Two things changed as a result: the gap was narrowed to the sub-200-person no-ERP buyer (gap 6.0 → 7.5), and the output was reframed from a PO tracker to a build-risk list with a paid concierge pilot as the first sale (wedge 6.5 → 7.5, market_pull 7.0 → 8.0). Akisto was found late and is the reason gap is capped at 7.5.

Investor signals weighed: YC's "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (the direct fit — AI doing the expeditor's coordination work), YC "Data Center Supply Chain" (produced candidate 5, parked as an expansion market because the sales cycle is too long for this builder), YC "AI for City Hall" (rejected: too close to past idea Backcheck and no narrow wedge found), a16z American Dynamism "renaissance of the American factory" and "AI-native industrial base" (used as evidence that the buyer population is growing, not as the idea), a16z "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" (supports the no-ERP, non-Silicon-Valley-stack framing), a16z "Systems of record lose ground" (supports selling a workflow layer to a buyer who has no system of record at all).
Sharpening (7.2 to 7.8): Round 1 — weakest criterion: gap (6.0). The first shape was a generic "AI expeditor chases your suppliers", which collided head-on with SourceDay, Didero, Leverage AI and HappyRobot. Change to the idea: drop everyone with an ERP and sell only to the sub-200-person, no-ERP hardware buyer, with email-forwarding as the only onboarding path. Research (deep pot + sharpen call on SourceDay/Morsa, then Didero/Leverage) found the segmentation holds: SourceDay entry ~$30k/yr with portal-adoption complaints on G2; Didero explicitly "mid-market and enterprise", 100+ deployments, ERP overlay; Leverage explicitly mid-market on SAP/NetSuite/Dynamics/Epicor/Infor with quote-only pricing. None publishes a self-serve small-team tier. Gap 6.0 → 7.5. But the same pot surfaced Akisto (SF, founded 2026, "Coming Soon" site, pilot on 2,000+ POs) doing nearly this mechanic, which is why gap stops at 7.5 and not 9.

Round 2 — weakest remaining: wedge (6.5) and market_pull (7.0). Change to the idea: move the output from "PO tracker" to "which build slips", and anchor the first version on a forwarded-email inbox so there is zero integration work and a pilot can be sold before the product exists. Research (sharpen calls on willingness-to-pay and on hwstartups forum evidence) found the labour prices that make the pitch concrete — VAs at $520-1,600/month, Wing procurement assistants at $999/$1,599, outsourced procurement at $8-25/PO, coordinator job posts at $62-72k and expeditor at $44-55k, all public and all above a $499/month price — and found first-person forum complaints about months-late machined parts and weeks of supplier chasing. It also found the honest limit: no source shows a sub-200-person team already paying for software in this category, so market_pull 7.0 → 8.0 (named role, confirmed adjacent budget) rather than 9, and wedge 6.5 → 7.5 (weeks to a first version, confirmed workaround price, but the first paid customer is still unproven). Pain 7.5 → 8.0 on the FMA 84% OTD figure plus the paid-workaround evidence.

Project:
prototype_summary: An interactive three-panel prototype where clicking messy supplier emails updates a live PO table with extracted evidence and confidence rules, rolling up into a ranked Monday build-risk list.
